question: Pipe P can fill (3)/(7) part of a tank in 12 hours, and pipe Q can fill (5)/(6) part of the same tank in 10 hours. Both P and Q were kept open for 2 hours, then both were closed. Pipe R alone was then opened and it emptied the water in the tank in 5 hours. Pipes P, Q and R together can fill the empty tank in:
solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Time for P to fill the tank = 12 × 7/3 = 28 hours. Time for Q = 10 × 6/5 = 12 hours.

Total capacity = LCM(28, 12) = 84 units. Efficiencies: P = 3 units/hour, Q = 7 units/hour.

P and Q operate for 2 hours → 2 × (3 + 7) = 20 units filled.

R empties 20 units in 5 hours → R's efficiency = −20 ÷ 5 = −4 units/hour.

Combined efficiency (P + Q + R) = 3 + 7 − 4 = 6 units/hour.

Total time to fill the tank = 84 ÷ 6 = 14 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 14 hours.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

P fills 3/7 part in 12 hours.

Q fills 5/6 part in 10 hours.

P and Q are kept open for 2 hours, then closed.

R alone empties the filled water in 5 hours.

**Formula Used:**

Total Work = Efficiency × Time

**Time required to fill complete tank:**

⇒ Time taken by P = 12 × (7 ÷ 3) = 28 hours

⇒ Time taken by Q = 10 × (6 ÷ 5) = 12 hours

**Calculations:**

⇒ Combined efficiency of P and Q = 3 + 7 = 10 units/hour

⇒ Water filled by P and Q in 2 hours = 10 × 2 = 20 units

⇒ Pipe R empties these 20 units in 5 hours

⇒ Efficiency of R = −20 ÷ 5 = −4 units/hour (emptying)

⇒ Net efficiency of P, Q, and R together = 3 + 7 − 4 = 6 units/hour

⇒ Time taken by P, Q, and R together to fill the empty tank = Total Work ÷ Net Efficiency

⇒ Time taken = 84 ÷ 6 = 14 hours

**∴ The correct answer is 14 hours.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Fractional Work to Full Time

If a pipe fills a fraction (a/b) of a tank in x hours, the time taken to fill the entire tank is calculated as x × (b/a) hours.

Inlet vs Outlet Pipes

Pipes that fill the tank are known as inlet pipes (represented with positive efficiency), while pipes that empty it are outlet pipes (represented with negative efficiency).

Combined Efficiency Method

When multiple pipes operate together, their net efficiency is the algebraic sum of their individual efficiencies. The formula to find the total time is: Total Work ÷ Net Efficiency.
